label: Headline
text: Scale to billions. Ship in seconds. Pay for the hours somebody used.
context: Three claims. The first is the one the funding deck's critique called a scaling hypothesis, not a result.

label: Lede
text: The CARLOS platform is the deployment substrate underneath every app on the framework. Every app starts with one channel, edge: run carlos deploy and it's live in seconds, no promotion step. Canary channels are there whenever you want a second opinion first, and a staged rollout — per-channel bake windows, a passkey, sign-off from more than one person — is one command away the day you want it, never before. Let idle apps sleep to a bucket for nothing and wake in milliseconds. It is open source and self-hostable — and it is also the engine under Carloku, if you would rather not run boxes.
context: Five sentences, 95 words, under the headline. The wordiest lede on the site.

label: Section heading
text: Every multiplier traces to a mechanism
context: Above four big-number tiles.

label: Standfirst
text: Not adjectives — line items. Each claim below names the machinery that produces it, so you can check it rather than believe it.

label: Tile 1 heading (10⁹ people)
text: Scale to billions
context: The tile's big figure is 10⁹ people.

label: Tile 1 body
text: Every person gets their own instance with its own database. A crash, a leak or a runaway query takes down one person's process; the next request restarts it and nobody else notices. Growing means adding boxes to the fleet, not architecture to your app.

label: Tile 2 heading (100× build speed)
text: Build faster

label: Tile 2 body
text: AI is the factory. Extravagant machines are spent at build time — at length, under tests that fail the build — to produce one lean artifact. The compute is spent once, at the factory; what ships stays small forever.

label: Tile 3 heading (1000× performance)
text: Query without a network hop

label: Tile 3 body
text: SQLite is compiled into the process, so a query is a function call and your data lives next to your compute: microseconds where a round trip costs milliseconds. Even a sleeping instance wakes in milliseconds.

label: Tile 4 heading (30× cheaper)
text: Cheaper, and more efficient with it

label: Tile 4 body
text: Most software is used a few hours a week and billed for all 168. On CARLOS an idle app hibernates to object storage — a few objects in a bucket, no process, no memory, costing nothing — and wakes on the next request. Less compute standing idle is also less energy burned for nothing.

label: Section heading
text: From branch to live, without a rebuild
context: Above the deploy rail diagram (canary/pr-142 → edge).

label: Standfirst
text: One artifact, one pointer by default. What you tested is what ships, because it is the same bytes.

label: Item heading
text: A live URL for every branch

label: Item body
text: Push a branch and get a canary URL in seconds: a real deployment on the real platform, not a localhost preview. Send it to a teammate before the code review starts.

label: Item heading
text: One command to serving

label: Item body
text: carlos deploy ships, promotes, and returns only when the URL is provably serving the new build — the edge names the version it serves and the command checks. Exit 0 means refresh and it is there.
context: 'carlos deploy' is set in code.

label: Item heading
text: A staged pipeline is one command, opt-in

label: Item body
text: carlos pipeline init --template edge-production gives an app more channels, each with its own bake window and approval rules; --template full-ladder is the old fixed canary → edge → beta → stable ladder, still there for anyone who wants it. Either way, promotion only ever points an existing channel at bytes you already shipped — nothing is rebuilt to get there.
context: Commands set in code.

label: Item heading
text: Rollback is a pointer move

label: Item body
text: Point the channel back at the previous release and the bleed stops. Immediate, no rebuild, no waiting. Going backwards is never new code.

label: Section heading
text: Safe to deploy, and safe to be deployed to

label: Standfirst
text: The default is live the moment you ship — the platform's job is to make that boring. Want a frightening step to guard against instead, on your own terms? That's a pipeline you opt into, not one you're stuck with.

label: Item heading
text: A bake window, when you ask for one

label: Item body
text: Give a channel --bake 72h and a new release must sit on it for that long before the channel's instances adopt it, so a compromised publisher cannot rush a poisoned build across your fleet. Deploys to an app's default edge channel carry no bake — they're live as soon as the header proves it — and canary channels never do either; the window is something you add per channel, through carlos pipeline. Rollback always skips the bake: pointing back at a hash that already served traffic takes effect immediately.
context: Two paragraphs on the page; shown here as one string.

label: Item heading
text: Residency, enforced below your code

label: Item body
text: Declare where your data lives — per app, or per customer instance — and a host outside that region will never claim it. There is no "just this once during a failover" path: no eligible host means the wake fails loudly instead of quietly relocating. Sleeping data rests in region-scoped buckets too, so residency covers rest as well as execution. Enforced by the platform, not promised in a policy PDF.
context: Two paragraphs on the page.

label: Item heading
text: Placement follows declared trust, not just capacity

label: Item body
text: Each workload publishes what a host can learn by running it, and the platform will not place it somewhere less trusted than that declaration requires. The classes are on the framework page.
context: 'The classes are on the framework page' should now point at /trust/; say what the link text should be.

label: Item heading
text: When it breaks, it says why

label: Item body
text: carlos logs is one timeline: your app's own output merged with the platform's events about it — wakes, restarts, and the reason a wake failed — filterable, followable live with -f, and in the console. No server access required, because the answer comes to you.

label: Item heading
text: Recurring work, on an app that sleeps

label: Item body
text: A hibernating instance cannot run its own timer — the process is not there to fire it. So the platform keeps the clock. carlos schedule set declares the work once, -every 6h or a cron line in UTC, and at the due time the platform wakes the instance, POSTs the path you named with the token already in its environment, and holds it awake until your handler returns. A sync every six hours; reminders in the days before a date. 2xx means done, 5xx is retried with backoff, 4xx is your app declining and nothing retries. carlos schedule ls prints the next and last fire for every instance, so "did it run?" is a question you answer from your terminal.
